question.text: A bond is issued at a face value of Rs.100 and a coupon of 10% per annum. Subsequently, interest rates in the market increase. This bond is most likely to quote in the secondary market at:

answer.text: A price below face value (at a discount)
A price above face value (at a premium)
A price that depends only on the issuer's credit rating, not interest rates

explanation.text: The Logic: Bond prices and yields move inversely. When market interest rates rise above an existing bond's coupon, the bond's price falls below face value so that its yield rises in line with the prevailing market rate. The workbook's Chapter 2 sample question on a Rs.100 face-value, 10% coupon bond after a rate rise concludes the bond is likely to quote below face value. The Trap: A premium (option B) occurs when market rates are below the coupon. Par value (option C) occurs only when market rates equal the coupon. Credit rating matters (option D), but the question isolates the impact of an interest-rate increase, which by itself pushes the price down. Note: This is a direct application of the inverse price-yield relationship to a fixed-coupon bond when market yields move higher.
